title: Asking with eikö … ole
summary: Add the question ending -kö to ei: ei + -kö = eikö. Negative possession questions keep ole after the owner: Eikö sinulla ole palloa?
targetSkills: Fixed eikö ole in possession questions
objectives: Ask a negative possession question with eikö and ole.
Recognise the pattern, then produce it with the supporting words shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: Add the question ending -kö to ei: ei + -kö = eikö. Negative possession questions keep ole after the owner: Eikö sinulla ole palloa?
Use the same eikö and ole for all six owners. A negative question can express surprise or an expectation: “Don’t you have a ball?” It still asks about possession.

The noun takes the negative partitive form. For the regular words used here: pallo + -a = palloa, kirja + -a = kirjaa, auto + -a = autoa, kynä + -ä = kynää. Each complete form is shown when question formation is the target.
Hänellä can refer to a man or a woman. Sinulla addresses one person; teillä addresses a group in these tasks. Teillä can also address one person politely when that context is stated.
A negative statement becomes a question by changing ei to eikö and putting it first; keep ole and the supplied partitive noun.
keyPoints: Use one singular thing and the owner form shown by the prompt.

sections.title: Regular noun forms in these examples
paragraphs: These forms name the thing after ei ole. The prompts show the noun form whenever forming it is outside this lesson’s target.
keyPoints: kissa (“cat”) → kissaa (“a cat”): regular singular partitive
koira (“dog”) → koiraa (“a dog”): regular singular partitive
tyyny (“pillow”) → tyynyä (“a pillow”): regular singular partitive
peli (“game”) → peliä (“a game”): regular singular partitive

steps: Add the question ending -kö to ei: ei + -kö = eikö. The neutral-only word ei takes the front-vowel ending.
minulla means “I as the owner”. Put this owner between eikö and ole.
Keep ole after the owner and the shown partitive palloa (“a ball”) last.
Eikö remains fixed with sinulla. Do not replace it with etkö from a personal-subject sentence.
sinulla means “you as the owner” for one person. Put this owner between eikö and ole.
Keep ole after the owner and the shown partitive kirjaa (“a book”) last.
Hänellä can mean “he” or “she”; either meaning uses the same eikö … ole frame.
hänellä means “he as the owner” or “she as the owner”; this example uses “she”. Put this owner between eikö and ole.
Keep ole after the owner and the shown partitive koiraa (“a dog”) last.
Several owners still use eikö … ole, not emmekö … ole.
meillä means “we as the owner”. Put this owner between eikö and ole.
Keep ole after the owner and the shown partitive autoa (“a car”) last.
The group owner teillä leaves eikö … ole unchanged, not ettekö … ole.
teillä means “you as the owner” for a group. Put this owner between eikö and ole.
Keep ole after the owner and the shown partitive peliä (“a game”) last.
Heillä leaves eikö … ole unchanged, not eivätkö … ole.
heillä means “they as the owner”. Put this owner between eikö and ole.
Keep ole after the owner and the shown partitive kynää (“a pen”) last.
Changing the thing does not change the question word eikö.
minulla means “I as the owner”. Put this owner between eikö and ole.
Keep ole after the owner and the shown partitive kissaa (“a cat”) last.
The noun and ei each follow their own vowel rule; the noun does not choose the -kö in eikö.
meillä means “we as the owner”. Put this owner between eikö and ole.
Keep ole after the owner and the shown partitive tyynyä (“a pillow”) last.

commonMistakes: Attach -kö to ei, not to ole: Eikö sinulla ole palloa? Keep ole as a separate word.
Use fixed eikö with every owner, including groups; do not replace it with emmekö or eivätkö.
Keep the shown partitive noun after the negative question pattern: palloa, rather than pallo.

parts.formation: Ei + the question ending -kö = eikö. The front-vowel ending follows ei, independently of the noun.

parts.role: possessor: the person who has the thing
parts.formation: he has the learned possession form heillä; its -lla/-llä ending marks the possessor. Learn this pronoun form as a whole.
Negative possession keeps ole after eikö, with every owner.
pallo + -a = palloa. This is the singular partitive, the noun form used when possession is denied.

optionFeedback.Eivätkö minulla ole kynää?: Ei + -kö gives eikö. Possession keeps eikö and ole unchanged for every owner; the noun uses its supplied partitive form. This choice uses the wrong verb form.
